name: Formal Methods for Security
description: Formal verification, proofs, and verified implementations of security-critical systems and protocols.

uss.narrative:
The earliest listed work shows formal methods being pointed at two very different targets at once. On the systems side, "HeapHopper: Bringing Bounded Model Checking to Heap Implementation Security" (USENIX 2018) used bounded model checking to find exploitable heap-metadata bugs in real allocators, while on the protocol side "Modelling and Analysis of a Hierarchy of Distance Bounding Attacks" (USENIX 2018) extended the applied pi-calculus to reason about distance-bounding security symbolically. The same year, "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) pushed formal reasoning into a brand-new domain, certifying robustness properties of deep neural networks. So from the start the area split along three threads: verifying implementations, analyzing protocols, and certifying learned models.

The next shift, around 2019-2021, was toward fully verified implementations rather than just bug-finding. "VRASED: A Verified Hardware/Software Co-Design for Remote Attestation" (USENIX 2019) and "EverParse: Verified Secure Zero-Copy Parsers for Authenticated Message Formats" (USENIX 2019) delivered machine-checked code with end-to-end security proofs, and "IODINE: Verifying Constant-Time Execution of Hardware" (USENIX 2019) brought the same rigor to leakage-free hardware. This matured into verified low-level infrastructure: "Formally Verified Memory Protection for a Commodity Multiprocessor Hypervisor" (USENIX 2021) and "DICE*: A Formally Verified Implementation of DICE Measured Boot" (USENIX 2021) proved security of the trusted-computing base itself, while "ETHBMC: A Bounded Model Checker for Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2020) carried model checking into the blockchain world.

A parallel and increasingly automated protocol-analysis line ran alongside it. "A Spectral Analysis of Noise" (USENIX 2020) gave comprehensive automated proofs over an entire family of Diffie-Hellman key-exchange protocols, "A Tale of Two Headers" (USENIX 2020) formalized inconsistent web-framing defenses, and "SmartVerif" (USENIX 2020) pushed protocol-verification automation with dynamic proof strategies. This momentum carried into wireless and cellular standards, with "Formal Analysis and Patching of BLE-SC Pairing" (USENIX 2023) and "Sherlock on Specs: Building LTE Conformance Tests through Automated Reasoning" (USENIX 2023) turning specifications themselves into objects of formal scrutiny.

Today the field is broad, applied, and tightly coupled to deployed systems. It has reached post-quantum cryptography with "Formal verification of the PQXDH Post-Quantum key agreement protocol" (USENIX 2024), blended fuzzing with formal guidance in "HyPFuzz: Formal-Assisted Processor Fuzzing" (USENIX 2023), and moved from finding flaws to automatically repairing them in "TAPFixer: Automatic Detection and Repair of Home Automation Vulnerabilities based on Negated-property Reasoning" (USENIX 2024). Alongside continued work on cellular and Bluetooth specifications like "CellularLint" (USENIX 2024) and "Finding Traceability Attacks in the Bluetooth Low Energy Specification" (USENIX 2024), the area now spans verified clouds, hardware leakage models, neural-network certification, and natural-language specs, all sharing the common goal of replacing testing intuition with proof.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this NDSS collection took formal methods out of the seminar room and pointed it at systems people actually run. "ZEUS: Analyzing Safety of Smart Contracts" (NDSS 2018) tackled the fact that a smart contract cannot be patched once deployed, using abstract interpretation and model checking to catch safety bugs before money is at stake. The same year, "LTEInspector: A Systematic Approach for Adversarial Testing of 4G LTE" (NDSS 2018) applied model checking with a cryptographic protocol verifier to the 4G LTE control plane, showing that formal reasoning could surface real adversarial attacks in a deployed cellular standard. Together these set the pattern that dominates the area: take a high-stakes, hard-to-fix system and reason about it formally.

The following years broadened both the targets and the techniques. Cellular protocols became a recurring proving ground — "Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA" (NDSS 2019) exposed channel assumptions and session-confusion problems as 5G was being finalized, and "PHOENIX: Device-Centric Cellular Network Protocol Monitoring using Runtime Verification" (NDSS 2021) shifted from design-time proofs to runtime verification on the end-user device. Alongside protocols, the community pushed into foundations and correctness of implementations: "Establishing Software Root of Trust Unconditionally" (NDSS 2019) sought guarantees that hold without trust assumptions, while "Analyzing Semantic Correctness with Symbolic Execution: A Case Study on PKCS#1 v1.5 Signature Verification" (NDSS 2019) used symbolic execution to find not just low-level bugs but semantic flaws in crypto code. Authentication protocols also came under the microscope with "A Formal Analysis of the FIDO UAF Protocol" (NDSS 2021).

By the mid-2020s the toolkit matured and the targets grew more diverse. Bluetooth pairing became a case study in how far formal analysis can reach: "Extrapolating Formal Analysis to Uncover Attacks in Bluetooth Passkey Entry Pairing" (NDSS 2023) turned symbolic models into concrete new attacks, building on the earlier "The Bluetooth CYBORG" (NDSS 2021) human-machine AKE analysis. The scope widened to trusted execution and enclaves ("RR: A Fault Model for Efficient TEE Replication," NDSS 2023; "A Formal Approach to Multi-Layered Privileges for Enclaves," NDSS 2025), to reference-monitor tamper analysis ("TALISMAN," NDSS 2024), and to a unified symbolic account of a real VPN in "A Unified Symbolic Analysis of WireGuard" (NDSS 2024).

The most recent work shows two clear directions. Formal reasoning is being fused with machine learning — "PropertyGPT: LLM-driven Formal Verification of Smart Contracts through Retrieval-Augmented Property Generation" (NDSS 2025) uses an LLM to generate the very properties a verifier checks, closing the loop opened by ZEUS seven years earlier. And the classic protocol-analysis thread keeps finding fresh flaws in current standards: NDSS 2026 brings "WCDCAnalyzer: Scalable Security Analysis of Wi-Fi Certified Device Connectivity Protocols" and "Formal Analysis of BLE Secure Connection Pairing and Revelation of the PE Confusion Attack," which uncovers a new confusion attack in the latest Bluetooth Secure Connection pairing, while "Consensus in the Known Participation Model with Byzantine Faults and Sleepy Replicas" (NDSS 2026) extends rigorous analysis to modern consensus. The area today is defined by scaling formal analysis to messy real-world standards and by pairing proof engines with automated, AI-driven property discovery.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, all at IEEE S&P 2018, staked out the classic terrain of formal methods for security: reasoning rigorously about protocols and systems. DEEPSEC (2018) tackled one of the genuinely hard problems in symbolic analysis, deciding equivalence properties like indistinguishability rather than simple reachability, while "Distance-Bounding Protocols: Verification without Time and Location" (2018) and "A Formal Treatment of Accountable Proxying Over TLS" (2018) showed how to bring specific real-world protocols under formal scrutiny. Alongside these, AI2 (2018) hinted at a new frontier, using abstract interpretation to certify robustness of neural networks, showing the field's toolbox reaching beyond traditional protocols.

The biggest shift over 2019-2020 was from verifying designs on paper to verifying implementations that actually run. "Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic" (S&P 2019) proved you could generate cryptographic arithmetic that was verified yet fast enough for deployment, and EverCrypt (S&P 2020) scaled this into a whole verified crypto provider; "The Last Mile" (2020) and "Formally Verified Cryptographic Web Applications in WebAssembly" (2019) pushed the same assurance out to optimized machine code and browser runtimes. In parallel, two new application areas exploded: smart-contract safety, with VerX (2020), VERISMART (2020), and executable Solidity semantics (2020) attacking the arithmetic and functional bugs draining real money; and microarchitectural security, where Spectector (2020) gave speculative-execution leakage a precise semantics in the wake of Spectre.

By 2021-2022 the field was both consolidating and deepening. "SoK: Computer-Aided Cryptography" (S&P 2021) mapped the whole machine-checked-crypto landscape, while "Hardware-Software Contracts for Secure Speculation" (2021), "High-Assurance Cryptography in the Spectre Era" (2021), and "SoK: Practical Foundations for Software Spectre Defenses" (2022) turned the ad-hoc Spectre response into principled contracts and defenses. Verified systems grew more ambitious with "A Secure and Formally Verified Linux KVM Hypervisor" (2021) and the CHERI design-and-proof effort (2020), and the core tooling matured, "ProVerif with Lemmas, Induction, Fast Subsumption" (2022) and the interactive computational-model prover (2021) letting proofs reach larger protocols and even standards like EMV (2021) and Bluetooth (2022).

The most recent work shows formal methods aimed squarely at large, deployed, messy systems. At S&P 2026, "Automated Formal Analysis of Signal's Double Ratchet" and "DY* Unchained" bring composable proofs and precise compromise modeling to the messaging protocols billions of people use, while "The Secrets Must Not Flow: Scaling Security Verification to Large Codebases" and "C-Verifier" (analyzing cross-service flaws in AWS Cognito) push verification to industrial-scale code and cloud identity. Hardware and consensus are equally in view, with "Interplay of Efficient Model Checking and Secure Processor Design" (2026) revisiting secure speculation via model checking and "Mechanized Safety and Liveness Proofs for the Mysticeti Consensus Protocol" (2026) verifying a modern DAG-based consensus. Together with "From Control to Chaos" (2025) on 5G access control and the hybrid EasyCrypt approach (2025) that blends deductive and circuit-based reasoning, the trajectory is clear: from verifying small protocols and primitives to formally reasoning about the full, deployed security stack.

ccs.narrative:
Formal methods for security at CCS has expanded from protocol verification toward hardware, smart contracts, and compiler correctness. A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) set the tone for the dataset period: using Tamarin and ProVerif to find gaps in the 5G AKA protocol before widespread deployment. 5GReasoner: A Property-Directed Security and Privacy Analysis Framework for 5G Cellular Network Protocol (CCS 2019) extended this to cross-layer properties, discovering new attacks the standard had missed.

Smart contract verification arrived with eThor: Practical and Provably Sound Static Analysis of Ethereum Smart Contracts (CCS 2020), which provided a sound abstract interpreter for EVM bytecode. Machine learning safety was formalized in Quantitative Verification of Neural Networks and Its Security Applications (CCS 2019), linking verification with robustness certificates. InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis (CCS 2020) brought formal analysis to bear on CPU-level leakage.

Secure compilation against microarchitectural adversaries was formalized in Exorcising Spectres with Secure Compilers (CCS 2021), which defined the threat model and proved that specific compilation strategies are sound. EasyPQC: Verifying Post-Quantum Cryptography (CCS 2021) extended the EasyCrypt proof assistant to cover post-quantum scheme security proofs, keeping formal verification pace with the post-quantum migration.

milestones.note: First rigorous formal analysis of 5G AKA using automated protocol verifiers, identifying unproven security goals.

milestones.note: Designed a processor architecture that enforces information-flow security with formal timing guarantees.

milestones.title: eThor: Practical and Provably Sound Static Analysis of Ethereum Smart Contracts

milestones.title: InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis
milestones.note: Used formal analysis to both discover Spectre gadgets and verify the correctness of mitigations.

milestones.title: Exorcising Spectres with Secure Compilers
milestones.note: Proved that specific compiler mitigations are formally sound against a full microarchitectural Spectre attacker.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list (2018) already spans the two poles that still define the field: verifying protocols and verifying implementations. On the protocol side, "A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication" (CCS 2018) and "LTEInspector" (NDSS 2018) took symbolic provers and model checkers to live cellular standards, while "DEEPSEC" (S&P 2018) advanced the underlying theory of deciding equivalence properties. In parallel, a large smart-contract thread opened with "ZEUS: Analyzing Safety of Smart Contracts" (NDSS 2018), and a separate strand applied formal methods to machine learning safety in "AI2" (S&P 2018) and "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018). Even low-level systems got attention through "HeapHopper" (USENIX 2018) and "HyperFlow" (CCS 2018).

The 2019-2020 period is where verified implementations became genuinely practical. "Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic" (S&P 2019) showed machine-checked crypto could be readable and fast, and "EverCrypt" (S&P 2020) and "The Last Mile" (S&P 2020) delivered whole verified, high-speed cryptographic providers; "EverParse" (USENIX 2019) and "VRASED" (USENIX 2019) extended proofs to parsers and remote-attestation hardware. Smart contracts matured fast in the same window, with "VerX" (S&P 2020), "VERISMART" (S&P 2020), "eThor" (CCS 2020), and "ETHBMC" (USENIX 2020) pushing sound and precise verification. Meanwhile Spectre reframed the microarchitectural frontier: "Spectector" (S&P 2020) and "InSpectre" (CCS 2020) gave principled semantics for speculative leakage.

By 2021 the area was consolidating. "SoK: Computer-Aided Cryptography" (S&P 2021) systematized a decade of tools, "Hardware-Software Contracts for Secure Speculation" (S&P 2021) turned Spectre defenses into checkable contracts, and proofs reached real systems and deployed standards in "A Secure and Formally Verified Linux KVM Hypervisor" (S&P 2021), "The Provable Security of Ed25519" (S&P 2021), and "The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify" (S&P 2021). "Clockwork Finance" (S&P 2023) then broadened smart-contract analysis from code safety to economic security.

The most recent work (2026) shows the field applying its now-mature toolchain to messy, high-stakes real systems while scaling up. Protocol analysis targets deployed messaging and wireless standards in "Automated Formal Analysis of Signal's Double Ratchet" (S&P 2026), "Formal Analysis of BLE Secure Connection Pairing" (NDSS 2026), and "WCDCAnalyzer" (NDSS 2026), each pairing new attacks with proofs of the fixes. Verification is stretching to large codebases and cloud identity in "The Secrets Must Not Flow" (S&P 2026) and "C-Verifier" on AWS Cognito (S&P 2026), to consensus protocols in "Mechanized Safety and Liveness Proofs for the Mysticeti Consensus Protocol" (S&P 2026), to secure-speculation processor design in "Interplay of Efficient Model Checking and Secure Processor Design" (S&P 2026), and even to legal-compliance reasoning in "Breaking the Illusion: Automated Reasoning of GDPR Consent Violations" (S&P 2026) - a sign the area has moved from proving isolated primitives to reasoning about whole deployed systems.
